items.stem: Which of these numbers is irrational? 22/7, 3.14, √9, π
items.markingKey: π cannot be written as a fraction of two integers; its decimal never ends and never repeats. 22/7 and 3.14 are rational approximations; √9 = 3. [1]

items.stem: Explain why √50 is not a whole number.
items.answer: 7² = 49 and 8² = 64, so √50 lies between 7 and 8 and cannot be a whole number.
items.markingKey: M1 compares with 49 and 64; A1 conclusion between 7 and 8. [2]

items.stem: Explain why every recurring decimal is a rational number.
items.answer: A recurring decimal can always be written as a fraction a/b (e.g. 0.333... = 1/3), and any number that can be written as a fraction of integers is rational.
items.markingKey: B1 can be written as a fraction; B1 link to definition of rational. [2]

items.answer: (a) Side = √120 and 120 is not a square number. (b) 10 and 11 (c) 11.0 cm

items.stem: What can you say about the decimal expansion of an irrational number?
options: It never terminates and never repeats
items.answer: It never terminates and never repeats
items.markingKey: An irrational number cannot be written as a/b with a, b integers, so its decimal expansion neither terminates nor recurs. [1]

items.stem: Zara says: "√6 and √24 are both irrational, so √6 × √24 must also be irrational." Show that Zara is wrong.
items.answer: √6 × √24 = √144 = 12, which is rational, so the product of two surds need not be irrational.
items.markingKey: M1 √6 × √24 = √144; A1 = 12, rational, so the claim is false. [2]

items.stem: Show that √2 × √18 is a rational number.
items.answer: √2 × √18 = √36 = 6, which is an integer and therefore rational.
